strengths: Soundness: The marginal/conditional decomposition is mathematically informative. Proposition 1 and Corollary 2 explicitly characterize the posterior-approximation and consistency terms, and the rate-distortion analysis clarifies why the proposed and mixture-based objectives favor different behavior.

Originality: Combining arbitrary modality masking with learnable permutation-invariant or equivariant aggregation is a useful extension beyond fixed PoE/MoE rules. The treatment of shared and modality-private latent variables is particularly thoughtful.

Significance: The approach addresses a practical limitation of multimodal VAEs: supporting many conditioning subsets without learning exponentially many separate encoders. SumPooling and SelfAttention often improve internally comparable likelihood results across the synthetic and MNIST-SVHN-Text experiments.

Evaluation: The paper tests linear models, identifiable nonlinear simulations, missing modalities, and a three-modality benchmark. It reports likelihood, latent recovery, coherence, classification, and rate-distortion metrics, exposing genuine trade-offs rather than claiming dominance on every metric.

Presentation: The conceptual motivation is generally clear, the manuscript contains substantial derivations, and the authors honestly acknowledge that mixture-based objectives can be preferable for cross-modal reconstruction.

Reproducibility and ethics: Architectures, principal training hyperparameters, importance-sampling particle counts, dataset sizes, and compute type are documented. The datasets are synthetic or standard digit/text benchmarks, and I found no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central object is not generally a variational lower bound. Corollary 2 contains an expectation of log(q_phi(z|x_S)/p_theta(z|x_S)) whose sign is unrestricted, as Remark 3 concedes. It becomes a true bound only under an encoder-consistency condition that is neither guaranteed nor empirically measured. Thus the title and repeated claims of a 'tighter variational bound' overstate what is established; higher objective values need not mean tighter likelihood bounds.

Soundness: The identifiability result is largely inherited from Lu et al. and assumes an exact posterior in a strongly exponential family, an injective decoder, and a full-rank variability condition. The paper does not prove that the proposed objective or aggregation architectures attain these assumptions, so the theorem offers limited support for claims that the method itself improves identifiability.

Experimental evidence: Most controlled gains are on data generated from favorable latent-variable assumptions. The only real benchmark is MNIST-SVHN-Text, and it shows mixed downstream results: the proposed objective is often worse in cross-reconstruction, conditional coherence for some directions, and latent classification. No substantive application with heterogeneous real-world modalities is provided.

Experimental evidence: Comparisons with external methods are not controlled because decoder variances and other settings differ; the paper itself notes that their likelihood values are not directly comparable. Important baselines such as MoPoE are therefore not retrained under the common architecture and likelihood protocol.

Statistical support is incomplete. The number of repetitions is not consistently stated for MNIST-SVHN-Text, significance tests or confidence intervals are absent, and several conclusions rely on small differences relative to reported run variability. The PoE values around 10^35 in Table 1 reveal severe numerical failure yet are still included in the comparison.

Reproducibility: No usable code-release location is present in the manuscript, and seeds, preprocessing details, classifier-training details, and full evaluation protocols are incomplete. Page 63 visibly contains missing text or links in the implementation/assets discussion.

Reproducibility and correctness: Algorithm 1 conditions z_S on x_M rather than x_S. More seriously, Algorithm 2 appears to subtract the private full-encoder log-density twice while omitting the shared full-encoder term, and its prior term has unclear conditioning. These errors make the claimed unbiased private-latent estimator impossible to implement reliably from the paper.

Presentation: The 65-page manuscript is diffuse and contains numerous notation or editing problems, including references to Corollary 19 instead of Corollary 2, a malformed entropy definition, inconsistent descriptions of the noisy modality, typos, and crowded tables. The limitations section mentions computation and reconstruction trade-offs but does not foreground the central fact that the proposed objective is not generally a bound.

strengths: The distribution-matching decompositions provide a potentially useful perspective on marginal, conditional, and latent-space consistency in multimodal VAEs.
The permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant encoder constructions cover both shared and private latent variables and are compatible with arbitrary modality masks.

The experiments compare objectives and aggregation schemes under mostly shared architectures, and the rate-distortion analysis usefully reveals that likelihood, cross-modal coherence, and representation quality need not improve together.

The paper candidly acknowledges extra computation and cases where mixture-based objectives give better cross-reconstruction. The synthetic and standard benchmark data raise no substantial ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central “tighter variational bound” claim is not established. The proposed conditional objective is not generally a lower bound on log p_theta(x_notS|x_S), and Corollary 2/19 contains a residual expectation of log(q_phi(z|x_S)/p_theta(z|x_S)) with unrestricted sign. Thus the objective can lie above or below the model log-likelihood. Tightness additionally requires strong posterior-consistency assumptions that are neither enforced nor empirically verified.

Several mathematical and algorithmic errors materially undermine soundness. Appendix B states an incorrect equality for the conditional log-likelihood, omitting the usual variational-gap KL. Appendix A gives the wrong sign when decomposing the conditional joint KL, and Appendix C concludes with +D despite defining distortion as negative expected log-likelihood. These are not merely stylistic issues because they occur in arguments supporting the main interpretation.

The provided pseudocode is not reliable enough for reproduction. Algorithm 1 constructs z_S using x_M rather than x_S. Algorithm 2 omits private latents from the cross-modal reconstruction, repeats the full-private-encoder log-density term, and lacks the expected full shared-encoder denominator term. Its claimed unbiased gradient therefore does not match the stated objective.

The identifiability contribution is weakly connected to the proposed method. Proposition 15 is adapted from prior conditional-identifiability results and assumes an exact strongly exponential posterior, injective decoder, continuous observations, and a rank condition. The paper does not show that its objective or aggregation architecture satisfies these assumptions or yields identifiability during optimization; MCC on favorable synthetic generators is insufficient evidence.

The empirical scope is narrow: mostly synthetic data and one established MNIST-SVHN-Text benchmark. On that benchmark, gains are mixed—mixture objectives often improve cross-reconstruction and latent classification, no method dominates coherence, and the private-latent SelfAttention result does not favor the proposed objective.

Likelihood comparisons are insufficiently validated. Importance-sampling estimates use encoder-dependent proposals, so comparisons between aggregation schemes can conflate generative fit with inference quality; only 64 particles are used in one synthetic study and no convergence, effective-sample-size, or higher-particle analysis is reported. Repetition counts and statistical testing are also unclear for the principal real-data results.

The evaluation lacks important controlled baselines and ablations: contemporary multimodal methods are largely quoted from external papers with different settings, while there is no study of mask distribution, number of modalities, aggregation capacity/parameter count, compute cost, or the contribution of each objective term.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite detailed architecture tables: no code or artifact is provided, and seeds, benchmark repetition counts, preprocessing, likelihood weights, classifier training, hyperparameter selection, and exact runtime are incomplete. The erroneous pseudocode compounds this problem.

Presentation is substantially below publication standard. The 65-page manuscript is diffuse, contains many notation inconsistencies and typographical errors, and repeatedly describes an approximate, sign-indefinite objective as a bound. The limitations discussion is honest but does not acknowledge this central theoretical limitation or the evaluation/reproducibility weaknesses. No explicit ethics or dataset-license discussion is provided, although the experiments themselves appear low risk.
